summaries.example: Imagine your friend asks whether to tell a small secret. A rule might say, “Always tell the truth.” But what if telling the secret would hurt someone badly? A particularist says we should look carefully at all the details. A generalist says that rules or guiding ideas can help us decide, even when we must use judgment.
summaries.summary: Moral particularism and moral generalism are two traditions that disagree about the place of moral principles. Generalists think broad principles can explain what is right and can sometimes guide us. Particularists think moral judgment must be sensitive to the details of each situation and may not depend on a fixed set of rules. The debate is not just about whether rules exist. It also asks whether rules explain moral facts, how people gain moral understanding, and whether rules help or hurt decision-making. Some views allow flexible rules with exceptions, so the disagreement has many possible positions rather than only two simple choices.
key_ideas: Some people think moral rules are central to ethics. Others think the details of each case matter more than fixed rules.
A reason can work differently in different situations. Something helpful in one case might be unhelpful in another.
Rules may help people act fairly and predictably, but rules can also make people too rigid.
The disagreement includes questions about what morality is, how we learn it, and how we should use it.
summaries.why_it_matters: People often face choices where a simple rule does not seem enough. This debate helps us ask how to balance consistency with attention to real circumstances. It also helps explain why wise judgment may require experience, care, and noticing details. Thinking about these views can make us better at discussing difficult choices without pretending that every problem has one easy formula.

important_terms.definition: A broad idea about what makes an action right or wrong, or what gives us a reason to act.
The view that each situation may need careful attention, because a reason can change depending on the details.
The view that morality includes important general rules or patterns that can explain or guide actions.
Something about a situation that counts in favor of, against, or sometimes not at all for an action.

questions_to_think_about: Can a rule be helpful without solving every case by itself?
Can the same fact be a reason for an action in one situation but not another?
When might following a rule make a decision less fair?

summaries.example: Suppose a student promised not to reveal a friend’s private information. A generalist might say that promise-keeping is normally a moral reason, perhaps within a system of principles about trust and duties. A particularist asks whether the promise was made under pressure, whether revealing the information would prevent serious harm, and what other features of the case change the reason’s force. The promise may still count against disclosure, but its moral significance is not assumed to be identical in every context.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry examines a wide debate about whether morality requires moral principles. Generalism treats principles as central, but principles can have different roles: they may be standards explaining moral facts, guides for deliberation, or action-guiding standards that do both. Particularism also has several forms, ranging from denying principles altogether to claiming only that we should not rely on them in practice. A central argument for particularism is holism about reasons. A feature such as humor, loyalty, or promise-keeping may support an action in one context, lose its force in another, or even count against the action. Generalists reply that such context-sensitivity could be represented by complex, hedged, or defeasible principles. The epistemological debate asks whether moral knowledge resembles perception or practical skill, and whether reliable judgment in new cases presupposes moral structure. Semantic arguments ask whether competence with concepts such as justice or goodness commits us to principles; these arguments remain disputed. Practical arguments point to principles’ possible benefits for resisting self-serving exceptions, coordinating behavior, and sustaining accountability. Particularists warn that principles can encourage rigidity and force complex cases into inappropriate categories. The entry therefore presents a diverse set of arguments and intermediate positions rather than a single decisive conclusion.
key_ideas: The labels “particularism” and “generalism” cover several positions. Principles may be standards that explain, guides that help action, or both.
The leading particularist argument appeals to holism about reasons: context can alter whether a consideration counts as a reason and what direction or force it has.
Holism does not by itself prove particularism. Generalists argue that context-sensitive reasons may still be organized by complex or defeasible principles.

Particularist accounts of moral knowledge emphasize perception, sensitivity, and skill. Generalists argue that reliable judgment across unfamiliar cases may require an underlying pattern or principled structure.
The practical debate concerns reliability, flexibility, special pleading, predictability, cooperation, and interpersonal accountability.
Intermediate positions are possible: they may accept hedged principles, default principles, or principles as useful guides while denying that all moral truth can be captured by exceptionless rules.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate concerns how people should reason when moral situations are complicated. It challenges the assumption that either consistency or sensitivity must always win. A principle may protect against favoritism, support cooperation, and make accountability possible, yet a rigid principle may overlook morally important differences. Conversely, case-by-case judgment may respond intelligently to context but may be vulnerable to bias or inconsistency. Understanding the debate clarifies what moral reasoning is supposed to explain, how moral learning works, and how individual judgment relates to shared standards.

important_terms.definition: A general moral claim intended to explain why actions, considerations, or traits have moral significance, or to guide action.
The position that morality does not depend on a suitable stock of moral principles, in one influential formulation; other versions are more limited.
A family of positions that gives moral principles a central role, whether as explanations, action-guides, or both.
The view that a consideration may be a reason in one context but not another, or may support an opposite conclusion in a different context.
A factor that blocks a consideration from functioning as a reason in a case.
A background condition that allows a consideration to function as a reason.
A moral principle or generalization that normally holds but can fail when relevant circumstances intervene.
The claim that moral judgment depends on noticing and responding appropriately to particular situations, often through developed experience or practical wisdom.

questions_to_think_about: Does the possibility that a reason can change with context show that no moral principles exist, or only that principles must be qualified?
What would make a principle a good explanation rather than merely a true general statement?
Can moral expertise be understood as a skill without reducing it to rule-following?
Are public principles necessary for holding one another accountable?
Would rules make moral decisions more reliable, or might they distort attention to the case?

summaries.example: Your class has a rule: students should not use another person’s work without permission. During a group project, one student copies a partner’s notes after the partner says it is fine. Later, another student copies someone’s work while pretending it is their own. A generalist may say that rules about honesty and permission help explain why the cases differ. A particularist may focus first on the details: permission, deception, fairness, and the effects on the people involved. Both views can allow judgment; they disagree about how much moral thinking should depend on general principles.
summaries.summary: Moral particularism and moral generalism are competing traditions about the role of principles in ethics. A generalist thinks principles can explain moral truth, guide decisions, or perform both jobs. A particularist argues that moral judgment must respond to the details of each case and may not depend on a complete set of principles. The debate becomes clearer when we separate different meanings of “principle.” A principle might state what makes an action right, offer practical advice, or do both. Particularists often defend holism about reasons: a fact that supports an action in one situation may have no force, or opposite force, in another. For example, telling a joke may help lighten a mood, but the same joke may be a reason against speaking if it would seriously offend someone. Generalists reply that this kind of context-sensitivity could still be organized by qualified or defeasible principles. The entry also examines how people gain moral knowledge. Some views compare moral judgment to perception or skill, while generalist arguments suggest that reliable judgment in unfamiliar circumstances may depend on patterns. Other arguments concern the meanings of moral concepts and the practical value of principles. Principles may help resist self-serving exceptions, make behavior more predictable, and support accountability. Particularists worry that principles may encourage rigid thinking. The entry presents these arguments as an open philosophical dispute with several intermediate options.
key_ideas: Generalists and particularists disagree about principles, but neither label identifies only one exact theory.
Principles can be standards, guides, or both. A guide need not work like an automatic decision-making machine.
Particularists emphasize that context can change a reason’s force. Generalists answer that patterns involving reasons and contexts may still be expressed in principles.
Moral knowledge may involve something like perception or a learned skill rather than consciously applying a rule every time.
Principles might reduce bias, improve predictability, and support public accountability. Critics worry that they can produce inflexibility.
Some philosophers defend middle positions using default, hedged, or exception-sensitive principles.
summaries.why_it_matters: Moral decisions rarely arrive as neat exercises with every relevant fact labeled. This debate asks whether good judgment comes mainly from rules, from sensitivity to circumstances, or from a combination of both. It is useful for thinking about fairness: treating similar cases alike matters, but so can recognizing morally important differences. The discussion also connects personal judgment with social life, because shared principles may help people trust, criticize, and justify their actions to one another.

important_terms.definition: A general moral idea that may explain what makes something right or wrong, or may help someone decide what to do.
The family of views that gives principles a significant role in moral explanation, moral guidance, or both.
The family of views that questions whether moral principles are needed, available, or useful for understanding and deciding moral cases.
The idea that a consideration’s moral role depends on its setting; it may support, oppose, or fail to affect an action in different cases.
A principle that usually applies but can be overridden or blocked by important circumstances.
A reason that counts in favor of an action, even if it may not settle the final decision by itself.
The ability to judge what matters in a situation and respond well, developed through experience and understanding.
The unfair practice of making an exception for oneself that one would not accept for other people.

questions_to_think_about: If a rule has exceptions, is it still useful as a moral principle?
Is noticing what matters in a case more like seeing, learning a skill, or following a rule?
Can public rules prevent people from making excuses for themselves?
When does flexibility become unfair inconsistency?
Could a person be both particularist about moral standards and generalist about useful moral guides?
